You pay tribute for storage, music, video, and AI.
Every month the tribute comes due, and you are still at the mercy of the gods.
So you decide to bring it all home, AI included.
It's so easy to start, you wonder why everyone doesn't do this themselves.
Then the problems arise. Networking, security, updates, backups.
A laptop at home is a start, until the lights go out.
Virtual machines share one host, so when it falls, they all fall.
A rented server survives your power cut, but it's still one machine.
By hand, staying up means balancing, health checks, and replication.
A failover you've never tested is only a prayer.
Then drift creeps in. Quick fixes leave no two machines alike.
Change one thing with no review and no rehearsal, and the tower falls.
Kubernetes is the all-seeing answer, but it's built for engineering teams.
Anything you only have one of is a single point of failure.
Two machines at your altar give you local high availability.
Machines at a friend's altar add regional high availability.
Optional failover into AWS, Google, or Azure makes it global.
Each level adds cost and complexity, so choose what your apps need.
What if your machine god patched itself, healed itself, and kept to the plan?
It updates one machine at a time, so the rest keep serving.
If an app fails, it restarts. If a machine fails, its apps move.
The plan is written in Git, and anything that strays is called back.
A scrying screen shows what's healthy, and your AI oracle mends the rest.
Boot the installer, and a blank machine awakens and joins the cluster.
Now your apps just run, your weekends are yours, and so is your money.
So how does Adaetum pull this off?
It invents nothing. It wires proven tools together, and runs them for you.
Here is what each one does, and why it earned its place.
Rocky is the stable base. Ansible keeps every machine configured the same.
RKE2 is hardened Kubernetes. Longhorn replicates your data.
Gitea holds your plan. Argo CD makes the cluster match it.
OpenBao is the vault. External Secrets deliver each app only its own.
Authentik gives one login. Kubewarden checks every change.
cert-manager renews certificates. One front door gives every app an address.
Tailscale is private VPN access. Cloudflared is public access.
Prometheus watches the cluster. Kured reboots one machine at a time.
A small agent runs on every machine, even if the cluster is down.
Now, what happens when things go wrong?
Machine dies: traditionally a 3 a.m. page. Adaetum moves apps.
A failed disk means a backup restore, if one exists. Adaetum's Longhorn keeps copies.
An app crashes. Often unnoticed. Adaetum restarts it and alerts you.
A bad change goes out. Typically no way back. Adaetum reverts the commit.
Hand edits cause drift. Adaetum prevents it and restores known states.
An expired certificate causes an outage. Adaetum renews it before it expires.
Leaked passwords are hard to trace and stop. Adaetum rotates them from one vault.
Updates due. Conventionally, downtime. Adaetum patches one at a time.
The vault restarts. By default, sealed. Adaetum unseals itself.
Adding a machine traditionally means a weekend of wiring. Adaetum joins it itself.
Remove a machine: drain it. Adaetum relocates its apps.
An attacker knocks. Commonly, open ports. Adaetum: none, one sign-in, all logged.
A server is lost. Classically, rebuilt from memory. Adaetum rebuilds from the plan.
A service provider causes an outage. Adaetum keeps running locally.
When an app gets busy, you buy a bigger box. Adaetum adds copies, then removes them.
Now, how does it all start?
On your computer, you run one command: task init. It walks eight steps.
Step one: a private recovery repository. Never a fork.
Step two: it signs into Cloudflare and Tailscale, and makes scoped keys.
Step three: you pick a domain and a tailnet. One public file, no secrets.
Step four: it finds and verifies the Rocky Linux installer.
Steps five to eight: validate, publish, build the installer, test delivery.
GitHub holds and builds. Cloudflare delivers and routes. Tailscale connects.
Three credentials, three lifetimes, and secrets never touch a command line.
Write the installer to USB, boot a blank machine, and walk away.
At install time it fetches the payload, so config changes are always picked up.
After reboot it waits for a clock and network, then joins your tailnet.
It checks for a cluster. If one exists, it joins. Otherwise it starts one.
It downloads the build bundle, and works through nine numbered phases.
The phases build Kubernetes, storage, certificates, ingress, then the vault.
Secrets move from temporary files into the vault, the new authority.
Argo CD and Gitea go in, and Argo CD starts following Gitea.
The cluster proves it can run from Git before it carries on.
Last, an encrypted recovery kit, and its temporary authority burns.
